title: Great Expectations

subtitle.text: Mr. Jaggers came to Miss Havisham's to dine that night.
Miss Havisham did not join us, and Mr. Jaggers explained that she never let anyone see her eat or drink.
"She wanders during the night. That's when she gets something to eat."
Later we played cards with Estella and Miss Havisham, and it was agreed that I would meet Estella's coach when she came to London.
That night Mr. Jaggers and I stayed at the Blue Boar Inn.
I lay awake, thinking of Estella and wondering when she would begin to be interested in me.
The next morning at breakfast I resolved to tell Mr. Jaggers that I didn't think Orlick was the right sort of person to fill a position of trust at Miss Havisham's.
"Very good, Pip," said Mr. Jaggers when I had finished. "I'll go back today and pay him off."
I was alarmed that Mr. Jaggers was going to dismiss Orlick so quickly.
I even hinted that Orlick might be difficult to deal with.
"Oh no, he won't," said Mr. Jaggers. "I'd like to see him argue with me."
Later that day we traveled back to London together.
As soon as I arrived in the city, I sent a codfish and a barrel of oysters to Joe to apologize for not visiting him.
At Barnard's Inn I found Herbert having a cold supper.
He was delighted to welcome me back, and after eating we sat in front of the fire and talked.
"Herbert, I have something to tell you. I love—adore—Estella."
Instead of being surprised, Herbert said, "Of course I know [i@that@i]."
"How do you know that? I never told you."
"You didn't have to tell me. You've adored her ever since I've known you.
But now I must say something disagreeable to you.
Think of how she was brought up. Think of Miss Havisham. Think of how Estella is herself.
This may all lead to misery. Can't you forget her?"
An uncomfortable silence fell between us. Herbert got up and busied himself with tidying the room, putting chairs back where they belonged and straightening up books.
Finally he came back and sat down near the fire. "Now I must tell you something. I am engaged, but it's a secret."

"Yes, she lives with her father, an invalid. I've never seen him because he keeps to his room upstairs, but I've heard him constantly. He roars and he pounds on the floor with some frightful instrument."
"Oh yes, I constantly expect to see him. I never hear him without expecting him to come tumbling through the ceiling." Herbert laughed at his joke.
He told me that the moment he made enough money, it was his intention to marry this young lady.
As we stared at the fire, I thought about how difficult it was to make enough money.
The days passed, and one day when I was busy with my studies, I received a note in the mail.
Although I had never seen the handwriting before, I knew it was from Estella.
She said that she would be arriving in London the day after tomorrow and asked me to meet her coach!
If there had been time, I probably would have ordered several suits of clothes for this occasion.
But since there wasn't time, I had to be content with what I owned.
My appetite vanished and I knew no peace until the day arrived.
In her traveling dress, Estella seemed more beautiful than ever.
Her manner was more charming toward me than ever before.
We stood near the inn while she pointed out her luggage to me.
When it was all collected, I remembered that I knew nothing of her destination.
"I'm traveling ten miles to Richmond," she said. "I am to have a carriage and you are to take me. This is my purse and you are to pay my expenses from it."
I hesitated to take her purse.
"Oh, you must take the purse!" she insisted. "We have no choice, you and I, but to obey our instructions. We are not free to follow our own minds."
As she looked at me, I hoped there was some hidden meaning in her words.
"A carriage will have to be sent for, Estella. Will you stay here a little?"
"Yes, I am to stay here, and I am to drink some tea, and you are to take care of me."
She put her arm through mine as if that were part of the instructions too, and we went into the inn for some tea.
"Where are you going in Richmond?" I asked when we were seated at a table.
"I'm going to live at great expense with a lady who has the power to take me around and introduce me to a lot of people. How do you enjoy living with Mr. Pocket?"
"I live quite pleasantly there, at least . . . ," I hesitated, ". . . at least as pleasantly as I could anywhere away from you."
"You silly boy," Estella said quite calmly. "How can you talk such nonsense?"
And then she went on talking about Matthew Pocket and his family.
Apparently there were others in the family who regularly gave Miss Havisham bad reports about me.
But Estella said I should not worry because nothing could make Miss Havisham dislike me.
Estella, in fact, was entertained by the efforts of these relatives to discredit me.
She playfully gave me her hand and I put it to my lips.
"You ridiculous boy," she said. "You should have asked before you touched my hand."
I leaned down, and her calm face was like a statue's.
"Now," said Estella, gliding away the instant I kissed her cheek, "you are to take me to Richmond."
We got into a carriage and began our journey. When we passed through Hammersmith, I showed her where Mr. Matthew Pocket lived.
I said it wasn't far from Richmond and that I hoped I would see her sometimes.
"Oh yes, you are to come when you think it's proper. You have already been mentioned to the family."
"I'm surprised that Miss Havisham could part with you again so soon after your return from France."
"It's part of her plans for me, Pip," said Estella, sighing as if she were tired.
"I am to write to her constantly and see her regularly and report on how I'm doing."
That was the first time she'd ever called me by my name, and I treasured it.
We arrived at the house in Richmond all too soon. Two maids came fluttering out to receive Estella. The doorway soon absorbed her boxes.
She gave me her hand and a smile and was then absorbed into the house too.
After the door shut, I continued to stand there, looking at the house.
I thought about how happy I would be if I lived there with her.
Yet I knew I was never happy with her. I was always miserable.
With the check for nine hundred pounds in my pocket, I went to see Miss Skiffins' brother, who had arranged for Herbert's position at Clarriker's.
He brought Clarriker to me, and I had the great satisfaction of completing the arrangements for Herbert's partnership.
This was the only good thing I had done since I learned of my great expectations.
Clarriker informed me that his shipping business was steadily improving, and with the money from me, he would now be able to establish a small branch office in Egypt.
Herbert, in his new capacity as partner, would go out and take charge of it.
I felt as if my last anchor were loosening and I would soon be driven by the winds and the waves.
But I had some consolation knowing that Herbert would soon come home and tell me this news himself, little suspecting that I had been involved in it.
It was now March. My left arm was taking so long to heal that I was still unable to get a coat on. My right hand was tolerably restored.
One Monday morning, while Herbert and I were at breakfast, I received a note from Wemmick: [i@Burn this as soon as you read it. On Wednesday you might do something if you feel able to try it.@i]
Herbert and I considered what to do because my injury was now a real issue.
"I've thought it over," said Herbert. "Instead of taking a waterman to help us row, we should take Startop. He was my father's student and he likes us."
"But how much would you tell him about what we're doing?"
"Very little. He doesn't need to know until Wednesday morning that there's an urgent reason for getting Provis away. Where will you go with Provis?"
It seemed to me that the place didn't matter as long as Provis was out of England. Any foreign steamer that would take us would do.
Because foreign steamers left London at high tide, our plan was to get down the river earlier in the day and lie waiting in some quiet spot.
But we needed to know when a steamer would pass by.
After breakfast we went out to pursue our investigations and found that a steamer bound for Hamburg, Germany, would likely suit our purposes.
We also noted what other foreign steamers would leave London on the same tide.
I then went to secure passports while Herbert went to see Startop.
When we met again at one o'clock, I had the passports and Herbert had found Startop, who was willing to help us.
Herbert was going to Mill Pond Bank that evening to prepare Provis to meet us on Wednesday.
We would not communicate with Provis again until we took him on board my small boat.
When I went home, I found a letter, which had been delivered by hand:

[i@If you are not afraid, come to the marshes tonight or tomorrow night at nine. Come to the little house by the kiln if you want information regarding your uncle Provis. Tell no one. You must come alone. Bring this letter with you.@i]
I didn't know what to do. The worst was that I had to decide quickly or I would miss the afternoon coach, which would take me down in time for tonight.
Finally I decided to go because of the reference to Provis.
I left Herbert a note, saying that I had gone to visit Miss Havisham to see how she was faring, and then I hurried off for the coach.
It was dark before I arrived.
Avoiding the Blue Boar, where I might be recognized by someone, I went to another inn.
While my dinner was being prepared, I stopped briefly at Miss Havisham's and found that she was still very ill, though somewhat better.
Back at the inn, I was not able to cut my dinner because of my injured arm, so the landlord did it for me.
Not recognizing me, he entertained me with my own story—the popular local version that Pumblechook was my benefactor.
"Does this young man ever come back?" I asked about myself.
"Yes, but he never visits Pumblechook, the man who made him."
"Oh yes," said the landlord. "All the time."
I thought of long-suffering Joe and sweet-tempered Biddy, the ones who had the real right to complain about me.
I had never felt so remorseful about my thanklessness to Joe as that night when I heard about the brazen impostor Pumblechook.
After dinner I put on my coat and looked for the letter, but could not find it.
I had the uneasy feeling that I must have dropped it in the coach.
It was a dark night, though the full moon rose as I went out upon the desolate marshes.
I walked for another half hour before I approached the kiln and the little house.
I saw a light in the house and went in. There was a candle on the table but no one was there.
I stood just within the door, looking out into the night. Suddenly the candle went out and a rope was thrown over me from behind.
"Now I've got you!" said a voice.
"Who are you?" I cried, struggling as the man tied me up. "Help! Help!"
He struck a light and I was surprised to see Orlick.
"Do you recognize this?" Orlick picked up a gun decorated with brass that I had seen before at Miss Havisham's.
"You cost me that job. And you came between me and a young woman I liked."
Oh, Biddy! "What are you going to do to me?" I asked him.
"I'm going to kill you!" He leaned forward, staring at me. "You've been in my way ever since you were a child. And I'll tell you something else.
It was me who struck down your sister and left her for dead. But that's your fault.
You were always favored while I was bullied and beaten. You did that, and now you're going to pay for it."
I thought of crying out again, but I knew no one could hear me. My arms burned from the rope tied tightly around them.
"And I'll tell you one more thing," said Orlick. "It was me you tripped over that night on your stairs.
I've had a mind to kill you since you were down here for your sister's funeral.
I've followed you everywhere and when I looked for you, I found your uncle Provis!"
He held the candle close to my face and I turned away.
"I know his name is Abel Magwitch." He grinned malevolently. "Beware Compeyson. Beware the gallows."
He picked up a heavy hammer and I shouted out with all my might.
I struggled and suddenly I heard voices and saw men attacking Orlick.
He got free of them, leaped over the table, and flew out into the night. And then all went black and I knew no more.
